verifiedClaims.claim: If you have filed a personal injury claim in Georgia or South Carolina, there is a real chance that an insurance company has hired a private investigator to watch you. This is not paranoia. It is standard operating procedure for insurers looking to reduce the value of your claim or deny it outright.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Insurers commonly use surveillance on injury claims; no primary source quantifies how often. Keep the warning, drop 'standard operating procedure' as a stated fact.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Ellenberg v. Pinkerton's, Inc., 130 Ga. App. 254 (1973), quoted in Anderson v. Mergenhagen (Ga. Ct. App. 2007): 'Reasonable surveillance is recognized as a common method to obtain evidence to defend a lawsuit.'
verifiedClaims.note: The Georgia Court of Appeals itself calls surveillance 'a common method' of defending a lawsuit, which supports 'common'; nothing supports 'standard operating procedure' or any frequency figure.

verifiedClaims.claim: Insurance companies spend billions of dollars each year on claims investigations, and private surveillance is one of their most effective tools for doing it.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The Coalition Against Insurance Fraud's 2022 study puts the cost of insurance fraud in the United States at $308.6 billion a year, which is why insurers fund special investigation units and surveillance.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Coalition Against Insurance Fraud, The Impact of Insurance Fraud on the U.S. Economy (2022)
verifiedClaims.note: No primary source states what insurers spend on investigations. CAIF publishes the fraud-cost figure ($308.6B, Colorado State University Global study, 2022, first update to the 1995 figure). Replace the spending claim with the cost figure and attribute it; 'one of their most effective tools' is opinion and can stay unattributed.

verifiedClaims.claim: This is not limited to large cases. Insurers have been known to deploy PIs on claims worth $25,000 or less when they suspect fraud or exaggeration.
verifiedClaims.note: No primary source for the $25,000 threshold. Keep 'This is not limited to large cases' and end the sentence there, or cut both.

verifiedClaims.claim: If you told the insurer you cannot lift more than ten pounds, and the PI records you loading a case of water into your trunk, that footage will appear in your claims file within 24 hours.
verifiedClaims.note: The '24 hours' timing is unverifiable. Keep the example, drop the time claim ('that footage goes straight into your claims file').

verifiedClaims.claim: Even a "like" on a friend's hiking photo has been used in depositions to suggest a claimant is more active than they admit.
verifiedClaims.note: No reported opinion or primary source located for this anecdote. Cut the sentence.

verifiedClaims.claim: "Sub rosa" is a Latin term meaning "under the rose" — in secret.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Standard dictionary sense; no legal source needed
verifiedClaims.note: Language fact, not a legal or statistical claim.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia regulates private investigators under the Georgia Private Detective and Security Agencies Act, codified at O.C.G.A. § 43-38-1 et seq. This statute requires all private investigators operating in Georgia to hold a valid license issued by the Georgia Board of Private Detective and Security Agencies.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Anyone 'desiring to engage in the private detective or private security business' in Georgia must apply for and hold a license (O.C.G.A. § 43-38-6(a)); the licensing board is the Georgia Board of Private Detective and Security Agencies, a professional licensing board under the Georgia Secretary of State.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 43-38-6 (Justia, 2025 Code); Georgia Secretary of State, Georgia Board of Private Detective and Security Agencies
verifiedClaims.note: Chapter 38 is titled 'Operators of Private Detective Businesses and Private Security Businesses'. The license requirement is § 43-38-6, not § 43-38-1 (the short-title section); cite § 43-38-6 for the licensing sentence. § 43-38-6(a) licenses the business/operator; investigators employed by a licensed agency are registered through the agency rather than individually licensed, so 'all private investigators ... hold a valid license' is an overstatement — say 'must be licensed by, or registered with, the Board'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Photograph and video record you in public — Georgia is a one-party consent state for recordings in public spaces. There is no expectation of privacy when you are visible from a public area, even if you are on your own property. If your front yard is visible from the street, a PI can record you there.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62(2) makes it unlawful to use a device to 'observe, photograph, or record the activities of another which occur in any private place and out of public view' without consent; activities visible from a public vantage point are not 'out of public view'. One-party consent (§ 16-11-66(a)) is a rule about intercepting conversations, not about video in public.
verifiedClaims.note: The sentence conflates two rules. Rewrite: 'Georgia law only bars recording activities that occur in a private place and out of public view (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62(2)). If your front yard is visible from the street, a PI can record you there.' Move the one-party-consent point to the conversation paragraph.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62, Georgia's wiretapping and eavesdropping statute, it is a felony to intercept or record private communications without the consent of at least one party to the conversation.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62(1) makes it unlawful 'in a clandestine manner intentionally to overhear, transmit, or record ... the private conversation of another which shall originate in any private place'; § 16-11-66(a) exempts a person who is a party to the communication or has one party's prior consent; § 16-11-69 makes a violation a felony punishable by one to five years' imprisonment or a fine of up to $10,000, or both.
verifiedClaims.note: Substance is right; the citations are incomplete. The one-party-consent rule lives in § 16-11-66, and the felony classification in § 16-11-69, not in § 16-11-62. Cite all three.

verifiedClaims.claim: A PI cannot bug your phone, record your private conversations from outside your window, or use electronic devices to listen to what you say inside your home.
verifiedClaims.note: (1) clandestine recording of a private conversation in a private place; (3) going on or about the premises of another to eavesdrop or secretly observe; (4) secretly intercepting a message sent by telephone or other private communication. Note for the writer: § 16-11-62(8), the GPS-tracker paragraph, only applies when the tracked person holds a protective order against the person placing the device — do not add a general 'no GPS trackers' claim for Georgia.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia also recognizes the tort of intrusion upon seclusion. If a PI uses extreme or invasive methods to gather information — peering through your windows with a telephoto lens, for example — you may have a separate legal claim against the investigator and the insurance company that hired them.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia recognizes intrusion upon seclusion (Anderson v. Mergenhagen, 283 Ga. App. 546, 642 S.E.2d 105 (2007): repeated following and photographing can be an unreasonable intrusion; physical trespass not required). But Georgia courts allow 'reasonable surveillance' of a claimant, including of a residence from a public road to investigate a disability claim; only surveillance 'conducted in a vicious or malicious manner ... or deliberately calculated to frighten or torment the plaintiff' is actionable (Ellenberg v. Pinkerton's, Inc., 130 Ga. App. 254 (1973)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Anderson v. Mergenhagen, 283 Ga. App. 546, 642 S.E.2d 105 (2007), quoting Ellenberg v. Pinkerton's, Inc., 130 Ga. App. 254, 202 S.E.2d 701 (1973)
verifiedClaims.note: Add the case citation and the Ellenberg limit so the paragraph does not overpromise; 'the insurance company that hired them' as a co-defendant is not addressed by these cases — say 'potentially against the investigator and the insurer' or drop the insurer.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina regulates private investigators under S.C. Code § 40-18-10 et seq., which requires licensure through the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 40-18-70(A) ('A person who desires to operate a private investigation business in this State must apply for a Private Investigation License from SLED'); § 40-18-30(B); SLED, Private Investigators
verifiedClaims.note: Chapter 18 of Title 40 is 'Private Security and Investigation Agencies'. The operative license section is § 40-18-70; '§ 40-18-10 et seq.' is acceptable for the chapter.

verifiedClaims.claim: The licensing requirements in South Carolina are broadly similar to Georgia's, but there are differences in enforcement and scope.
verifiedClaims.note: Unsupported filler; no source compares enforcement. Cut the sentence or reduce to 'Both states license the business, not just the individual.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Use video and photographic equipment in public — South Carolina does not prohibit recording individuals in public spaces where there is no expectation of privacy.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 17-30-20 (reaches only wire, oral and electronic communications); no South Carolina statute bars video of a person in public view
verifiedClaims.note: Stated as an absence of prohibition, which is accurate.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina's wiretapping law at S.C. Code § 17-30-20 makes it illegal to intercept wire, oral, or electronic communications without the consent of at least one party. Like Georgia, South Carolina is a one-party consent state, meaning a PI can record a conversation they are part of but cannot secretly record conversations between other people.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: S.C. Code § 17-30-20 makes it a felony to intentionally intercept a wire, oral or electronic communication; § 17-30-30(C) makes it lawful 'for a person not acting under color of law to intercept ... where the person is a party to the communication or where one of the parties to the communication has given prior consent'; § 17-30-50(A) sets the penalty at up to five years' imprisonment or a fine of up to $5,000, or both.
verifiedClaims.note: Substance correct; cite § 17-30-30(C) for the one-party rule (it is not in § 17-30-20) and, if the paragraph keeps the felony parallel with Georgia, § 17-30-50 for the penalty.

verifiedClaims.claim: One area where South Carolina differs from Georgia is in its treatment of trespass. South Carolina courts have generally held that entering someone's private property — even briefly — to conduct surveillance can constitute criminal trespass. PIs operating in South Carolina tend to be more cautious about staying on public property because the case law on trespass-related surveillance is less forgiving than in some other states.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Both states criminalize trespass. Georgia: O.C.G.A. § 16-7-21(b) (entering the land or premises of another without authority for an unlawful purpose, or after notice that entry is forbidden; misdemeanor). South Carolina: § 16-11-600 (entry after posted or given notice; misdemeanor, up to $100 or 30 days) and § 16-11-620 (entering premises after warning or refusing to leave; up to $200 or 30 days). Georgia also makes it a separate offense to go on or about another's premises to eavesdrop or secretly observe (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62(3)).
verifiedClaims.note: No South Carolina opinion supports a 'stricter' or 'less forgiving' trespass rule for surveillance, and no source supports Georgia's 'tolerance for brief incursions'. On the statutes, Georgia's § 16-7-21(b)(1) (entry 'for an unlawful purpose', no notice required) and § 16-11-62(3) are if anything broader than South Carolina's notice-based misdemeanors. Replace the paragraph with the two-state statement in currentValue.

verifiedClaims.claim: Recording Consent | One-party consent (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62) | One-party consent (S.C. Code § 17-30-20)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: One-party consent (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-66) | One-party consent (S.C. Code § 17-30-30)
verifiedClaims.note: Comparison-table row. Both cited sections are the prohibitions; the consent exceptions are § 16-11-66 and § 17-30-30.

verifiedClaims.claim: Trespass Enforcement | Standard trespass laws apply; some tolerance for brief incursions | Stricter enforcement; courts less tolerant of PI trespass even briefly
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Criminal Trespass | Misdemeanor — entry for an unlawful purpose or after notice (O.C.G.A. § 16-7-21) | Misdemeanor — entry after notice or warning (S.C. Code §§ 16-11-600, 16-11-620)
verifiedClaims.note: Comparison-table row. Replace the invented contrast with the statutes.

verifiedClaims.claim: Personal Injury SOL | 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) | 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530)
verifiedClaims.note: Matches the authoritative jurisdiction table.

verifiedClaims.claim: Comparative Fault Rule | Modified — barred if 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) | Modified — barred if 51% or more at fault
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Modified — barred if 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) | Modified — barred if more than 50% at fault (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243 (1991))
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g); Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991); profiles/writer-profile.md Jurisdiction rules
verifiedClaims.note: § 51-12-33(g): 'the plaintiff shall not be entitled to receive any damages if the plaintiff is 50 percent or more responsible'. The South Carolina cell is correct on substance ('51% or more' equals 'more than 50%') but has no authority; add Nelson. Never cite § 15-38-15.

verifiedClaims.claim: Social Media Monitoring | Public posts are accessible; no "friending" under false pretenses | Public posts are accessible; ethical rules restrict deceptive access
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Public posts are accessible; a lawyer, and an investigator working at a lawyer's direction, may not gain access by deception (Ga. Rules of Professional Conduct 5.3, 8.4) | Public posts are accessible; same rule under S.C. Rules of Professional Conduct 5.3, 8.4 (Rule 407, SCACR)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: State Bar of Georgia, Georgia Rules of Professional Conduct (Rules 5.3, 8.4); S.C. Appellate Court Rule 407, Rules 5.3 and 8.4
verifiedClaims.note: The row implies the two states differ; they do not. Both states' Rule 8.4 bars conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation, and Rule 5.3 makes lawyers responsible for investigators they direct. Neither state has a statute or a formal advisory opinion specifically on pretextual 'friending'; the rules bind lawyers and their agents, not an insurer-hired PI acting without counsel. Georgia rules: https://www.gabar.org/general-counsel/georgia-rules-of-professional-conduct

verifiedClaims.claim: Both states allow extensive public surveillance, but South Carolina's stricter approach to trespass means that PI evidence obtained from private property is more likely to be challenged successfully in South Carolina courts.
verifiedClaims.note: Depends on the unsupported trespass contrast. Keep 'Both states allow extensive public surveillance' and cut the rest.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia claimants should be aware that the shorter two-year statute of limitations under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 puts additional pressure on cases — insurers may drag out investigations hoping you miss the deadline. South Carolina's three-year window under S.C. Code § 15-3-530 provides slightly more time, but delays still hurt your case.
verifiedClaims.note: Deadlines match the authoritative table.

verifiedClaims.claim: A PI cannot enter your home, your fenced backyard, your garage, or any other private space without your permission. They cannot climb fences, open gates, or walk onto posted property. If they do, the evidence they gather may be inadmissible, and they may face criminal charges.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Entry is criminal trespass in both states (O.C.G.A. § 16-7-21; S.C. Code §§ 16-11-600, 16-11-620), and in Georgia going onto another's premises to secretly observe is a separate offense (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62(3)). Georgia excludes evidence obtained in violation of its eavesdropping part (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-67); no comparable automatic exclusion exists for footage obtained by simple trespass, so 'your attorney can move to exclude it' is the accurate framing.
verifiedClaims.note: Add the statute citations; 'may be inadmissible' is hedged enough to keep, but tie it to § 16-11-67 (Georgia) and § 17-30-65 (South Carolina) which apply to secretly observed/intercepted material, not to trespass alone.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under both O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62 and S.C. Code § 17-30-20, intercepting private communications without consent is a crime. A PI cannot tap your phone, hack your email, place a listening device in your car, or record conversations you have inside your home through a window or wall.
verifiedClaims.note: Both statutes reach these acts; § 16-11-62(4) covers intercepting 'a message sent by telephone, telegraph, letter, or by any other means of private communication'.

verifiedClaims.claim: PIs cannot represent themselves as police officers, federal agents, or any other government official. This is a criminal offense in both states.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: falsely holding oneself out as a peace officer, officer of the court or other public officer with intent to mislead is impersonating an officer, punishable by a fine of up to $1,000 or one to five years' imprisonment, or both (O.C.G.A. § 16-10-23). South Carolina: representing oneself as a law enforcement officer and acting on it is a misdemeanor, up to $500 or one year (S.C. Code § 16-17-720).
verifiedClaims.note: Add the two citations. 'Federal agents' is governed by federal law (18 U.S.C. § 912), not verified here; either drop 'federal agents' or leave it uncited. South Carolina's statute is limited to law enforcement officers and requires acting on the representation (arrest, detain, search or 'in any way impersonate'), so 'any other government official' overstates it for South Carolina.

verifiedClaims.claim: If someone flashes a badge and claims to be a detective investigating your accident, ask for identification and a business card. A legitimate PI will identify themselves if pressed.
verifiedClaims.note: No statute verified requiring a PI to identify themselves on request; the advice to ask for identification can stay, but 'A legitimate PI will identify themselves if pressed' is unsupported. Cut that sentence.

verifiedClaims.claim: Your medical records are protected by HIPAA and state privacy laws. A PI cannot call your doctor's office, walk into a hospital, or contact your pharmacy to obtain your treatment records. The only way an insurer can access your medical records is through a signed authorization from you or a court order. If a PI obtains medical information through deception, that evidence can be suppressed and the PI can face serious legal consequences.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule a provider may release your records only with your valid written authorization (45 CFR 164.508) or under legal process: a court or administrative order, or a subpoena or discovery request accompanied by satisfactory assurances of notice to you or a qualified protective order (45 CFR 164.512(e)(1)). Knowingly obtaining individually identifiable health information under false pretenses is a federal crime punishable by up to five years' imprisonment and a $100,000 fine (42 U.S.C. § 1320d-6(b)(2)), and since the 2009 HITECH amendment that liability reaches individuals, not just covered entities.
verifiedClaims.note: 'The only way ... is a signed authorization or a court order' omits the subpoena/discovery path in 164.512(e)(1)(ii), which is how insurers in litigation usually get records. 'Can be suppressed' is not a verified rule; say 'your attorney can move to exclude it'. 'Serious legal consequences' can be made concrete with § 1320d-6. HIPAA binds the provider (covered entity), which is why the PI cannot get records by calling — phrase it that way. 42 U.S.C. § 1320d-6: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1320d-6

verifiedClaims.claim: Both Georgia and South Carolina have anti-stalking statutes that apply to PIs just as they apply to anyone else.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia's stalking statute (O.C.G.A. § 16-5-90(a)(1): following, placing under surveillance or contacting a person without consent 'for the purpose of harassing and intimidating') contains no exemption for private investigators. South Carolina's harassment-and-stalking article expressly does NOT apply to 'a licensed private investigator performing services or an investigation as described in detail in a contract signed by the client and the private investigator pursuant to Section 40-18-70' (S.C. Code § 16-3-1700(G)); a PI who steps outside that contract, or an unlicensed one, is covered (stalking is a felony, up to five years, § 16-3-1730(A)).
verifiedClaims.note: FALSE as written for South Carolina. § 16-3-1700(G) carves licensed, contracted private investigators out of the stalking and harassment definitions. Rewrite the sentence so it is true of both states: Georgia's statute applies to anyone; South Carolina's exempts a licensed PI working under a signed client contract, so the remedy there is a complaint to SLED or a civil intrusion claim (Snakenberg v. Hartford Cas. Ins. Co., 299 S.C. 164, 383 S.E.2d 2 (Ct. App. 1989): 'watching, spying, prying, besetting, overhearing' can be an actionable intrusion when substantial and unreasonable). Georgia § 16-5-90: https://law.justia.com/codes/georgia/title-16/chapter-5/article-7/section-16-5-90/

verifiedClaims.claim: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, if the jury finds you were 50% or more responsible for your own damages — including through credibility issues raised by PI evidence — you recover nothing. In South Carolina, the threshold is 51%.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g), a plaintiff who is 50 percent or more responsible for the injury recovers nothing; in South Carolina a plaintiff more than 50 percent at fault is barred (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243 (1991)). Surveillance evidence goes to credibility and the extent of injury, which reduces damages; it bears on the fault percentage only where it concerns how the accident happened.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g); Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991); profiles/writer-profile.md Jurisdiction rules
verifiedClaims.note: The 50% / more-than-50% thresholds are right. The clause 'including through credibility issues raised by PI evidence' misstates how apportionment works: § 51-12-33(g) apportions responsibility for the injury, not belief in the plaintiff. Remove that clause; keep the (accurate) following sentence about credibility reducing recovery. Add the Nelson authority for South Carolina.

verifiedClaims.claim: Even private posts can be subpoenaed during litigation, but making your profiles private at least prevents casual monitoring by PIs and adjusters.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: General civil-discovery principle (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-34; S.C. R. Civ. P. 34)
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate as a general statement; 'obtained in discovery' would be more precise than 'subpoenaed' since a party's own posts are reached by a Rule 34 request, not a subpoena.

verifiedClaims.claim: Do not delete old posts. Deleting social media content after filing a claim can be considered spoliation of evidence, which can result in sanctions or negative jury instructions.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Phillips v. Harmon, 297 Ga. 386 (2015) (spoliation is 'the destruction or failure to preserve evidence' relevant to contemplated or pending litigation; duty arises when litigation is reasonably foreseeable); Kershaw County Bd. of Educ. v. U.S. Gypsum Co., 302 S.C. 390 (1990) (adverse-inference instruction when a party loses or destroys evidence)
verifiedClaims.note: Both states recognize the doctrine; the Georgia authority applies it to any party once litigation is reasonably foreseeable, which covers a claimant who has filed a claim. South Carolina: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1314502/kershaw-county-board-of-education-v-united-states-gypsum-co/

verifiedClaims.claim: If the PI obtained evidence through illegal means — trespassing, wiretapping, accessing medical records without authorization — your attorney can move to suppress that evidence. In both Georgia and South Carolina, evidence obtained in violation of the law or a party's constitutional rights may be excluded from trial.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Both states exclude illegally intercepted or secretly recorded communications by statute: 'No evidence obtained in a manner which violates any of the provisions of this part shall be admissible in any court of this state' (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-67); no intercepted communication or evidence derived from it may be received in evidence where its disclosure would violate the chapter (S.C. Code § 17-30-65(A)). Evidence obtained by trespass or by improper access to medical records has no automatic statutory exclusion; your attorney can move to exclude it and can pursue the investigator for the violation.
verifiedClaims.note: 'A party's constitutional rights' is misleading in a civil case: the constitutional exclusionary rule restrains government actors, not a private investigator. Replace with the two statutory exclusion rules, which are stronger and citable.

verifiedClaims.claim: In some cases, the insurer's use of PI surveillance crosses the line into bad faith. If an insurer uses misleading or out-of-context surveillance footage to deny a legitimate claim, your attorney may be able to pursue a bad faith claim against the insurance company. This can result in additional damages beyond your original personal injury claim.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Neither state lets an injured third-party claimant sue the at-fault party's liability insurer for bad faith. Georgia's bad-faith statute, O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, runs only to the policyholder, and the third-party provision, § 33-4-7, is limited to property-damage losses (Mills v. Allstate Ins. Co., 288 Ga. App. 257 (2007)). South Carolina 'does not recognize a third party action for bad faith refusal to pay insurance benefits' (Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131, 526 S.E.2d 218 (2000)). A bad-faith claim is available only against your own insurer on first-party coverage — uninsured/underinsured motorist, medical payments, or a workers' compensation carrier.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. §§ 33-4-6, 33-4-7; Mills v. Allstate Ins. Co., 288 Ga. App. 257, 653 S.E.2d 850 (2007); Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131, 526 S.E.2d 218 (2000)
verifiedClaims.note: As written the section promises a remedy that does not exist in the ordinary car-accident scenario the post describes (a claim against the other driver's insurer). Narrow it to first-party coverage (UM/UIM, med-pay, workers' comp) or cut the section. Mills: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ga-court-of-appeals/1190510.html ; § 33-4-6: https://law.justia.com/codes/georgia/title-33/chapter-4/section-33-4-6/

verifiedClaims.note: Accurate summary of both states' rules.

verifiedClaims.currentValue: In Georgia, private detective businesses must be licensed under O.C.G.A. § 43-38-6. In South Carolina, licensing is governed by S.C. Code § 40-18-70 and administered by SLED.
verifiedClaims.note: Same section-number correction as the key takeaways. This answer renders into FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: PIs can follow you in public places, photograph or video record your activities in public, monitor your social media accounts, conduct background checks using public records, and observe your home from public areas. They can document anything visible from a public vantage point. They cannot trespass, wiretap, hack accounts, impersonate law enforcement, or access your medical records.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. §§ 16-11-62, 16-7-21, 16-10-23; S.C. Code §§ 17-30-20, 16-11-600, 16-11-620, 16-17-720; Ellenberg v. Pinkerton's (surveillance of a residence from a public road is not an intrusion)
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate for both states.

verifiedClaims.claim: In public places, yes. PIs can take photos and video of your activities in any public setting without your consent. However, both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 17-30-20) prohibit recording private conversations without consent. A PI cannot record conversations inside your home or other private settings.
verifiedClaims.note: Correct. If the writer wants precision, 'without the consent of at least one party' (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-66; S.C. Code § 17-30-30(C)) — a PI who is part of the conversation may record it.

verifiedClaims.claim: Most people never know. Professional PIs are trained in covert surveillance techniques.
verifiedClaims.note: No figure is asserted; leave as is.

verifiedClaims.claim: Follow your doctor's orders strictly, avoid activities that contradict your injury claims, limit social media posting about your life and activities, do not exaggerate your injuries to anyone, and be honest with your attorney about your physical capabilities.
Your attorney can file motions to suppress evidence obtained through illegal means such as trespassing, wiretapping, or privacy violations.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Your attorney can move to exclude evidence obtained illegally. Secretly recorded or intercepted communications are inadmissible by statute in both states (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-67; S.C. Code § 17-30-65), and evidence gathered by trespass or other privacy violations can be challenged as well.
verifiedClaims.note: 'Suppress' is criminal-procedure vocabulary; in a civil case the statutory exclusion for intercepted communications is the citable rule, and trespass-obtained footage is challengeable rather than automatically excluded. This answer renders into FAQPage structured data.

recommendedEdits: Stalking sentence (What PIs Cannot Do > Harassment or Intimidation): rewrite so it is true of both states — Georgia's O.C.G.A. § 16-5-90 applies to anyone, but South Carolina's § 16-3-1700(G) exempts a licensed PI working under a signed client contract; point South Carolina readers to a SLED complaint or a civil intrusion claim (Snakenberg v. Hartford, 1989).

Filing Bad Faith Claims: narrow to first-party coverage (your own UM/UIM, med-pay or workers' comp carrier) — cite Mills v. Allstate, 288 Ga. App. 257 (2007) (§ 33-4-6 policyholder only; § 33-4-7 property damage only) and Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131 (2000) (no third-party bad-faith action) — or cut the section.

Replace the South Carolina trespass paragraph and the 'Trespass Enforcement' table row with the statutes for both states: O.C.G.A. § 16-7-21 (misdemeanor; entry for an unlawful purpose or after notice) and S.C. Code §§ 16-11-600, 16-11-620 (misdemeanor; entry after notice or warning); delete the 'stricter'/'more tolerant' contrast and the sentence 'South Carolina's stricter approach to trespass means ...'.
Comparison table, Recording Consent row: cite O.C.G.A. § 16-11-66 and S.C. Code § 17-30-30 (the consent exceptions), not § 16-11-62 and § 17-30-20 (the prohibitions).
Comparison table, Comparative Fault row (SC cell): add 'Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (1991)' and phrase as 'more than 50% at fault'; never cite § 15-38-15.

Comparison table, Social Media Monitoring row: make both cells the same — public posts are accessible; a lawyer and investigators working at a lawyer's direction may not gain access by deception (Rules 5.3 and 8.4 in both states).
Georgia wiretap paragraph: keep § 16-11-62 as the prohibition, add § 16-11-66 for the one-party-consent exception and § 16-11-69 for the felony penalty (one to five years or up to $10,000).
South Carolina wiretap paragraph: add § 17-30-30(C) for the one-party rule and § 17-30-50(A) for the penalty (up to five years or $5,000).

Georgia 'Photograph and video record you in public' bullet: replace the 'one-party consent state for recordings in public spaces' sentence with the actual rule — § 16-11-62(2) only bars recording activities in a private place and out of public view.

Georgia intrusion paragraph: cite Anderson v. Mergenhagen, 283 Ga. App. 546 (2007), and add the Ellenberg v. Pinkerton's limit (reasonable surveillance from a public road to investigate a disability claim is not an intrusion; only vicious, malicious or intimidating surveillance is).

Georgia licensing sentence, key takeaways and FAQ 1: cite O.C.G.A. § 43-38-6 (or '§ 43-38-1 et seq.') for the license requirement rather than bare § 43-38-1, and S.C. Code § 40-18-70 (or '§ 40-18-10 et seq.') rather than bare § 40-18-10; say 'licensed by, or registered with' the Georgia board since employees of a licensed agency are registered rather than individually licensed.

Opening paragraph: replace 'Insurance companies spend billions of dollars each year on claims investigations' with the attributed CAIF figure ($308.6 billion a year in insurance fraud, Coalition Against Insurance Fraud 2022 study); soften 'standard operating procedure' to 'common'.

Cut the unverifiable specifics: 'claims worth $25,000 or less', 'within 24 hours', the 'like on a friend's hiking photo' anecdote, 'A legitimate PI will identify themselves if pressed', and 'there are differences in enforcement and scope'.

HIPAA paragraph: add the subpoena/discovery path (45 CFR 164.512(e)(1)(ii)) alongside authorization (164.508) and court order; replace 'can be suppressed' with 'your attorney can move to exclude it'; make 'serious legal consequences' concrete with 42 U.S.C. § 1320d-6 (up to five years and $100,000 for obtaining health information under false pretenses).

Impersonation paragraph: cite O.C.G.A. § 16-10-23 and S.C. Code § 16-17-720; drop or leave uncited 'federal agents' (federal law), and note South Carolina's statute covers law enforcement officers specifically.

Comparative fault paragraph (At trial): delete 'including through credibility issues raised by PI evidence' from the § 51-12-33 sentence and add Nelson for South Carolina; keep the following sentence about credibility reducing recovery.

Challenging Admissibility and FAQ 6: replace 'evidence obtained in violation of the law or a party's constitutional rights may be excluded' with the statutory exclusions — O.C.G.A. § 16-11-67 and S.C. Code § 17-30-65 — and 'move to exclude' rather than 'suppress'.
Contact section: add North Charleston to the office list (client.json lists six offices).
